strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant vulnerability of CLIP models and proposes an appealing training-free intervention.

The empirical gains are substantial and consistent across five OpenCLIP scales: typographic-attack accuracy improves on all four evaluated attack datasets while ordinary classification accuracy generally changes by about one percentage point or less.
The evaluation includes synthetic and previously published typographic benchmarks, multiple clean datasets, and models ranging from ViT-B to ViT-BigG.
The attention manipulation experiment and analysis of CLS-to-CLS attention sinks are useful initial evidence that the selected heads influence sensitivity to written text.
The paper clearly acknowledges that its CLS-only intervention may not transfer to downstream systems that consume spatial tokens.
weaknesses: The evidence does not establish that the identified heads form a typography-specific circuit. The attention score is computed using text placed at a fixed bottom-center location, but there are no matched controls for position, high-contrast non-text patterns, fonts, text locations, or natural scene text. High scores could therefore reflect spatial or low-level visual biases.

The causal and mechanistic claims are overstated. Ablating heads selected by the proposed score shows that those heads affect the output, but the paper lacks random-head, layer-matched, attention-mass-matched, and alternative-importance baselines needed to demonstrate specificity. It also does not test whether the claimed circuit is sufficient for typographic behavior.

The intervention experiment is internally inconsistent: Equation 8 assigns alpha to CLS-to-CLS attention and 1-alpha to spatial attention, whereas Figure 5 and its caption assign 1-alpha to CLS attention and alpha to spatial attention. This makes the direction and interpretation of the central causal manipulation ambiguous.

The comparison is incomplete. Only Defense-Prefix is evaluated, despite several other relevant defenses being discussed. The proposed method substantially underperforms Defense-Prefix on most attack benchmarks, including 65.00% versus 82.78% on Disentangling, so the claim of competitiveness with the state of the art needs more careful qualification.

Evaluation rigor is limited: no confidence intervals, repeated runs, significance tests, or robustness to the circuit-construction subset and epsilon are reported. Probe training and validation details are also insufficient to rule out overfitting or leakage.

The circuit-selection algorithm stops at the first ranked head whose cumulative ablation exceeds the clean-accuracy threshold. This order-sensitive heuristic can miss useful later heads, yet it is not compared with other selection procedures or ablated over the threshold choice.

Preservation of general capability is assessed using only three object-classification datasets. There is no evaluation of retrieval, localization, OCR, natural-image text, calibration, or downstream multimodal applications, making the claims that the released models are broad drop-in replacements and suitable for safety-critical deployment unsupported.

Reproducibility is incomplete: although libraries, hardware, and a few hyperparameters are given, the manuscript does not provide sufficient implementation details, exact checkpoints, prompt templates, splits/seeds, circuit head identities, or a clearly accessible code/model artifact. Numerous notation, equation, caption, and typographical errors further reduce clarity.

strengths: The central idea—identifying typography-sensitive attention heads and selectively suppressing their CLS-token contributions—is intuitive, computationally lightweight, and potentially useful.

The evaluation covers five OpenCLIP model scales and reports sizable improvements on several synthetic and real-world typographic-classification benchmarks, generally with small changes on three clean datasets.

The layerwise probes, attention analyses, and controlled attention manipulations provide suggestive evidence that typographic information becomes concentrated in later layers and that a sparse subset of heads contributes to this behavior.

The paper is visually clear and acknowledges important limitations concerning spatial-token-based downstream systems and adaptive attacks. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/b5606c26b8c740b287bdd3978035d885/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central Typographic Attention Score is mathematically invalid as written: in Eq. 6, the attention value in the numerator and denominator cancels, making the score independent of the head and equal to a count of masked tokens. It is also unnormalized over the dataset and therefore cannot lie in [0,1], contrary to the text. Because this score determines the entire circuit ranking, the method is not reproducible from the paper.

The causal intervention is described inconsistently. Eq. 8 assigns alpha to CLS-to-CLS attention and 1-alpha to spatial attention, whereas the Figure 5 caption states the reverse. This ambiguity directly affects the interpretation of the principal causal experiment.

The evidence does not justify the broad safety and “drop-in replacement” claims. All reported tasks are zero-shot classification through the CLS token; there is no evaluation on the VLM jailbreaks, generative pipelines, retrieval systems, content moderation, or spatial-token consumers emphasized in the motivation. The paper itself concedes that the intervention may not affect systems such as LLaVA or IP-Adapter.

The security evaluation lacks an explicit threat model and any adaptive attack. Indeed, the authors note that an attacker may increase the selected heads’ spatial attention. Robustness to different fonts, sizes, positions, rendering styles, multiple text regions, natural scene text, and attacks optimized against the defended model is not systematically tested.

Baseline coverage is inadequate. Only Defense-Prefix is compared experimentally, despite the related-work section identifying several other relevant defenses. Defense-Prefix substantially outperforms the proposed method on two of the three typographic benchmarks in Table 4, and there are no comparisons with simple alternatives such as random-head ablation, later-layer ablation, attention-based text masking, or selecting heads by ablation effect.

The circuit-construction procedure uses labeled ImageNet-100 data and repeated accuracy evaluations to select a model-specific prefix of ranked heads. Thus, while gradient-free, it is not a calibration-free inference-time defense. The paper does not quantify this selection cost, test sensitivity to the calibration subset or epsilon, or show that circuits transfer across datasets or checkpoints.

The mechanistic claims are overstated. Attention concentration and destructive ablation establish neither that the selected heads uniquely encode typography nor that they form a coherent circuit. Missing controls include matched non-text patches, random or score-matched heads, head-output magnitude controls, activation patching, and tests of whether the same heads support benign OCR or other visual features.

Experimental reporting is insufficient for reproducibility and statistical assessment: exact pretrained checkpoints, preprocessing and prompt templates, typography-generation details, probe splits and optimization settings, random seeds, and uncertainty estimates are absent. Several real-world benchmarks contain only 110–1,000 examples, yet only point estimates are reported.

The manuscript contains numerous presentation and terminology problems, including repeated spelling/grammar errors, inconsistent alpha definitions, percentage-versus-percentage-point language, and use of “dyslexic” as a potentially stigmatizing label unrelated to the clinical condition. Overall, the promising idea is not supported with the precision, controls, and breadth required for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper presents a useful and intuitive mechanistic hypothesis: typographic information is concentrated in a relatively small set of later-layer attention heads that transmit information to the CLS token.

The proposed intervention is lightweight and requires no parameter optimization. Ablating only selected heads' CLS-token contributions is practically appealing and preserves clean accuracy much better than indiscriminate model modification would likely do.

Evaluation spans five OpenCLIP model scales and four typographic-attack datasets. The consistent robustness gains, including improvements of 6.1–32.8 points on real-world attack benchmarks and 13.1–19.6 points on ImageNet-100-Typo, are encouraging.
The evaluation includes three non-typographic datasets and shows that clean accuracy generally changes by approximately one point or less, supporting the claimed robustness–utility tradeoff.

The probe analysis, attention-score visualizations, attention-sink analysis, and controlled attention interventions collectively provide a coherent qualitative account of where typographic information emerges.
The limitations and misuse discussion appropriately acknowledges that the method modifies only the CLS pathway and may therefore offer limited protection for systems consuming spatial tokens.
weaknesses: The central claim that the selected heads constitute a causal typographic circuit lacks essential controls. The paper does not compare against random heads, matched later-layer heads, high-attention heads for non-text regions, or heads selected directly by clean-accuracy impact. Without these controls, it is unclear how much of the gain is specific to the proposed Typographic Attention Score.

The definition of the Typographic Attention Score in Eq. 6 appears to omit normalization over the dataset even though the score is subsequently treated as lying in [0,1]. More importantly, high attention to a text region does not by itself establish that a head writes typographic information; output-value or activation-patching analyses would provide stronger evidence.

The key causal experiment is internally inconsistent. Eq. 8 defines alpha as CLS-to-CLS attention, while Figure 5a and its caption assign 1-alpha to CLS attention and alpha to spatial attention. The reported direction of robustness as alpha increases consequently cannot be interpreted unambiguously.

Baseline coverage is insufficient for a top-tier empirical claim. Only Defense-Prefix is compared directly, on one model size, despite the related-work section identifying projection, fine-tuning/interpolation, and sparse-autoencoder defenses. Defense-Prefix is substantially stronger on several attack benchmarks, while the proposed method's main advantage is clean-data preservation.

The circuit-selection procedure depends on labeled ImageNet-100 control data, masked synthetic Unsplash data, and repeated model-specific evaluations. Thus, 'training-free' is technically accurate but understates the data and computational requirements. Selection also terminates at the first candidate exceeding the threshold rather than skipping it, making the resulting circuit sensitive to ranking noise and the arbitrary epsilon value; no sensitivity analysis is provided.

Several experimental details needed for reproducibility are missing, including exact OpenCLIP checkpoints and pretraining datasets, probe train/test construction and regularization, zero-shot prompt templates, synthetic text rendering parameters, random seeds, and uncertainty across dataset samples or circuit-construction splits.

The real-world Disentangling and PAINT-DS evaluations contain only 180 and 110 examples, respectively, yet no confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated runs are reported. This makes some cross-method and cross-model differences difficult to assess.

Clean evaluation does not measure the intended cost of the defense: degraded legitimate text understanding. Ordinary ImageNet-100, Food-101, and Aircraft images are insufficient to characterize performance on natural scenes where reading text is necessary. This weakens the claim that the released models are broadly suitable as safety-critical drop-in replacements.

The demonstrated defense is confined to zero-shot classification through the CLS token. No downstream VLM, retrieval, moderation, or generative-system experiment supports the broader application and safety claims made in the introduction and conclusion. Overall, the idea and initial results are promising, but missing causal controls, limited baseline comparisons, and protocol ambiguities place the work slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and practically relevant contribution: a gradient-free defense that identifies and suppresses a sparse set of CLIP attention heads associated with typographic sensitivity.

The mechanistic analysis is unusually actionable. Layerwise probes, the Typographic Attention Score, attention-sink manipulation, and targeted head ablation provide complementary evidence connecting particular heads to the transmission of typographic information into the CLS token.

The empirical scope is strong: results cover five OpenCLIP model scales, synthetic and real-world typographic benchmarks, standard classification datasets, OCR evaluation, and medical-domain models. Robustness gains are large and generally transfer beyond the ImageNet-100 data used to construct the circuits.
The paper explicitly measures important tradeoffs. Standard zero-shot accuracy is mostly preserved, while the substantial loss of OCR capability is quantified and appropriately acknowledged.

Comparisons with Defense-Prefix and OCR-based blurring are informative. In particular, reporting that blurring is stronger in absolute robustness prevents overstating Dyslexify's empirical advantage, while Dyslexify retains benefits in interpretability and inference-time overhead.
The method is simple to deploy, scales to billion-parameter encoders, and is accompanied by stated code and model releases, supporting practical reproducibility.
weaknesses: Circuit construction is not purely mechanistic: after ranking heads by attention score, the method repeatedly evaluates labeled ImageNet-100 and ImageNet-100-Typo accuracy to decide which heads to retain. This outcome-guided selection risks benchmark overfitting, and the paper does not compare against matched random-head, magnitude-based, or accuracy-greedy ablations to isolate the value of the proposed Typographic Attention Score.

Evaluation protocols are underspecified. The paper does not clearly state train/test splits for several reported results, how many random attack realizations are used, or whether circuit selection and evaluation samples are disjoint. This is especially concerning for ISIC2019, which appears to be used both to select the medical circuit and to report performance.

The baseline coverage is incomplete for the broad state-of-the-art positioning. Only Defense-Prefix is compared directly among learned/model-level defenses, and only on ViT-L; other cited defenses are not evaluated. The strongest tested baseline, OCR plus blur, outperforms Dyslexify on nearly every ImageNet-100-Typo setting.

The causal evidence is suggestive but incomplete. There are no matched control interventions, uncertainty estimates, repeated circuit-construction runs, or tests of circuit stability across typography locations, fonts, datasets, and seeds. Selecting circuit members partly by their observed accuracy effects also makes subsequent ablation gains less independent as causal validation.

The defense only modifies the CLS-token residual contribution. Many modern VLMs consume spatial tokens, so the experiments do not substantiate broad claims about jailbreak prevention, malicious generation, or suitability as a drop-in defense for general multimodal systems; this limitation is acknowledged but materially narrows the impact.

The synthetic threat model is limited to a few fonts and class-name overlays. There is no adaptive evaluation or systematic coverage of transformations such as stylized text, occlusion, curved text, multilingual text, multiple strings, or location/size variation. The claim that adaptive evaluation is infeasible because typography is non-differentiable is too strong, since black-box, search-based, or differentiable-rendering attacks remain possible.

Several technical and presentation issues need correction: the transformer update equations appear to place the MLP before attention without explaining a nonstandard convention; Figure 5's caption says increasing alpha raises spatial attention although alpha is defined as CLS attention and the main text states the opposite; and some medical dataset/task definitions are ambiguous. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported despite small real-attack benchmarks of only 110–1,000 examples.

strengths: The paper studies an important robustness problem: text embedded in images can strongly distort CLIP predictions, including in safety-sensitive settings.

The proposed intervention is simple and practically appealing: it requires no parameter training, targets only selected attention-head contributions to the CLS token, and incurs little apparent inference-time overhead.

Experiments cover five OpenCLIP model scales, several synthetic and real typographic-attack datasets, standard classification benchmarks, and a medical CLIP model. The reported robustness gains are generally large and transfer beyond the ImageNet-100 data used for circuit construction.

The paper acknowledges the substantial loss of legitimate OCR capability and includes a strong OCR-plus-blur baseline, runtime measurements, circuit-size statistics, and qualitative mechanistic analyses.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim is overstated. Attention localization, layerwise probe correlations, and behavioral changes under ablation show causal influence on predictions, but do not establish that the selected heads form a coherent circuit that specifically extracts and transmits typographic semantics. The greedy procedure explicitly selects heads according to attack accuracy, making improved behavior partly true by construction. Essential controls—random or magnitude-matched head ablations, alternative ranking criteria, position-attending heads, and tests of necessity versus sufficiency—are absent.

The Typographic Attention Score is estimated using text confined to the bottom two token rows. It can therefore select heads with a positional or low-level rendering bias rather than typography-specific functionality. The paper provides no systematic tests across text position, size, orientation, color, font, language, occlusion, or natural scene text to disentangle these explanations.

The defense evaluation lacks adaptive attacks. The assertion that adaptive evaluation is infeasible because typographic attacks are inherently non-differentiable is unconvincing: black-box search, discrete optimization, differentiable rendering, and simple searches over words and placements are all plausible. An attacker could also target unablated heads or downstream spatial tokens.

The method only suppresses selected contributions to the CLS token. The authors acknowledge that many contemporary VLMs consume spatial tokens, yet no downstream VLM, retrieval, generation, or content-moderation system is evaluated. This substantially undercuts claims about broad multimodal deployment and drop-in use in safety-critical applications.

Baseline coverage is inadequate. Defense-Prefix is compared only on ViT-L, while other related defenses discussed in the paper are omitted. More importantly, OCR plus blur consistently outperforms Dyslexify on the only benchmark where it is reported, with similarly small clean-accuracy changes; it is not evaluated on the real attack or medical datasets. Thus the practical advantage over straightforward preprocessing remains unclear.

The intervention imposes a severe capability tradeoff: OCR accuracy drops by roughly 8–30 percentage points. Clean performance is evaluated on only three ordinary vision datasets, so the claim that general visual capabilities are maintained is too broad, especially for natural images where text is genuinely informative.

The medical evidence does not justify the stated real-world safety implications. The attacks remain synthetic label overlays, the circuit is selected using a synthetic attacked medical dataset, and evaluation relies on accuracy without uncertainty estimates or clinically relevant sensitivity/specificity analysis. One dataset/column is also insufficiently defined.

Experimental reporting is incomplete: exact OpenCLIP checkpoints and pretraining sources are unclear; typographic-data generation lacks important rendering details; no confidence intervals, bootstrap analysis, or repeated-run variability is reported despite some attack sets containing only 110–1,000 examples; and the claim that small subsets yield nearly identical circuits is unsupported quantitatively.

There are technical and presentation inconsistencies. The transformer equations omit layer normalization and output projection and appear to reverse the usual attention/MLP order; the score definition sums over examples although reported values look averaged; and the discussion of the alpha intervention sometimes says increasing CLS attention increases spatial attention, contradicting its own equation. These issues make the exact intervention harder to validate and reproduce.

strengths: The paper presents an appealing and practically relevant idea: identifying attention heads associated with typographic sensitivity and ablating only their contribution to the CLS token, without fine-tuning or added inference-time preprocessing.

The empirical gains are substantial and broadly consistent across five OpenCLIP scales. Robustness improves on synthetic and real typographic benchmarks while ordinary zero-shot accuracy generally changes by less than one percentage point.
Evaluation on independently constructed real-attack datasets provides useful evidence that the selected intervention transfers beyond the synthetic ImageNet-100 data used for circuit construction.
The attention manipulation experiment provides meaningful causal evidence that the selected heads can control reliance on typographic information, going beyond purely correlational probing.

The medical-model experiments, OCR trade-off analysis, runtime measurements, circuit sparsity results, and comparison with an OCR-and-blur defense make the study unusually broad and help delineate where the method is useful.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic interpretation is not fully established. The Typographic Attention Score is computed using text placed in a fixed bottom-center region, so heads with an intrinsic positional bias toward that region may score highly even if they are not typography-specific. Clean-image, blank-overlay, relocated-text, and matched non-text controls are needed across all selected heads.

Circuit selection directly evaluates labeled ImageNet-100 and ImageNet-100-Typo performance after each candidate ablation. Consequently, the final circuit is partly discovered through benchmark-guided search rather than solely through the proposed mechanistic score. Random-head, score-only, accuracy-search-only, and alternative-ranking ablations would clarify what the score contributes.

Baseline coverage is limited. The main learned comparison is Defense-Prefix on only ViT-L, despite several related defenses discussed in the paper. Moreover, the included OCR-and-blur baseline is consistently stronger on ImageNet-100-Typo while preserving clean accuracy, substantially weakening claims of state-of-the-art or broadly preferable robustness.

No uncertainty estimates, repeated circuit-construction runs, or sensitivity analyses for text placement, font, size, color, attack phrase, epsilon, and the stopping parameter are reported. This makes the stability of the selected circuits and reported improvements difficult to assess.

The lack of adaptive evaluation is a major limitation for a defense paper. The assertion that adaptive attacks are infeasible because typography is non-differentiable is unconvincing: black-box search, discrete optimization, differentiable rendering, and systematic variation of placement or style are viable adaptive strategies.

The scope is narrower than some deployment claims suggest. The intervention modifies only the CLS stream, whereas many contemporary VLMs and generative systems consume spatial tokens; the paper does not demonstrate robustness in those downstream systems. OCR accuracy also falls by 8–30 percentage points, so these models are not general drop-in replacements.

Some technical presentation issues need correction: the displayed transformer update appears to place the MLP before attention, the Typographic Attention Score equation omits normalization by dataset size despite being presented as a percentage, and parts of the Figure 5 caption contradict the definition and accompanying results for alpha.

The medical threat is evaluated through synthetic label overlays rather than realistic clinical manipulation, and important details such as class mappings and evaluation protocol are underspecified. Thus, claims about tangible real-world medical risk and mitigation are stronger than the evidence supports.
